fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The path from festivals to birthkeeping", "body": "Elise Frosch tells Chance Garton how she went from a private Catholic upbringing in Louisiana, hula hooping at festivals and a sociology degree, to a trip to Nepal and yoga teacher training after a frightening psychedelic experience left her temporarily unable to see. A friend asked her to be a doula, a word she had never heard, and searching led her to the Matrona program in Georgia. What she expected to be clinical training turned out to be teaching on the physiology and the esoteric nature of birth, and it changed her life in four days."}, {"title": "Birth is not a medical emergency", "body": "Much of the hour is spent dismantling the idea that birth is a malfunction needing management. Elise recalls asking her sister, a neonatal ICU nurse, why the cord is cut immediately, and being told the baby must take a screaming first breath or the lungs will not develop. Chance calls that pure superstition, no different from a pitcher adjusting his cap before a game, and says the whole system runs on middlemen who frighten you into needing the expert. Elise adds that hospitals base their protocols on the average American, and she does not consider herself average."}, {"title": "What the hospital room actually does to labor", "body": "Elise walks through the standard sequence: triage, an IV placed just in case, monitors that limit movement, no food because a C section might be coming, and a clock that expects half a centimeter of progress every twenty to thirty minutes. When labor stalls, pitocin brings contractions without the hormones of natural labor, which hurt more, which leads to the epidural. Her argument is that birth is an altered state of consciousness, so bright lights and staff asking if you are okay every ten minutes pull a woman out of herself exactly when she needs to go in."}, {"title": "The unconscious desire to be a victim", "body": "Chance asks whether women have confused the real power of birth with the currency of martyrdom, and Elise says yes emphatically. She points to Yolanda Norris Clark and the Free Birth Society, and to Yolanda answering a question about her painless ninth birth by saying she released the unconscious desire to be a victim. Elise heard that while pregnant with Emanuel and it landed hard. She tells women carrying birth trauma that redemption is possible, but it starts with owning that on some level they agreed to it, a hard pill she knows many will refuse."}, {"title": "Two births and the mystery on the other side", "body": "The stories carry the argument. Elise labored three days with her first son at home while her mother, once appalled, brought grapes and watermelon and cut the cord. Her second, Manu, arrived in a bathroom with only James there, no midwife, no ultrasounds, after blood clots she chose to trust through. Chance closes by reading the C section as astro theology, Caesar and the sun leaving Virgo on December 25th, and by describing the mother crossing into the source realm as father, spirit and child at once, three becoming one."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Elise Frosch of Family Fungi joins InnerVerse to talk about her role as a sacred birth keeper. She helps us conceive answers to the most logical questions pertaining to birth, and we discuss why pregnancy is not a medical emergency, how to dispel fear narratives, the mother as spiritual psychopomp, perspective on the pains of labor, eliminating victim consciousness, and the story of her medically unsupervised home birth experience.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, Elise details the changes in body and mind during and after the 40 weeks, how not to impart the belief of original sin and brokenness to baby, talking to loved ones about circumcision, hospital SOPs, the mystery of the afterbirth, placentaphagy, and the divine twin spirit guardian.
